---
applyTo: "spec/requests/**/*.rb,spec/features/**/*.rb"
---

# Controller and route specs

- In `spec/requests`, name the top-level block after the controller's resource, e.g. `RSpec.describe "Posts"` for `PostsController`. Inside it, write one `describe` block for each route comment, in the same order as the controller. Name each block with its route, e.g. `describe "GET /posts/:id"`.
- Name request specs for nested controllers after the full controller name, e.g. `RSpec.describe "Posts::Comments"` in `spec/requests/posts/comments_spec.rb`. Name `describe` blocks with the parent's param, like the route comments, e.g. `describe "GET /posts/:post_id/comments"`.
- When a controller has custom actions, put their `describe` blocks in the request spec below the standard actions, in alphabetical order, the same as the controller, e.g. `describe "POST /posts/:id/duplicate"` then `describe "GET /posts/:id/preview"` after `describe "DELETE /posts/:id"`.
- Leave the controller's default format out of request spec `describe` names, e.g. `describe "GET /posts"`, not `describe "GET /posts.html"`, in a controller that serves HTML.
- When an action responds to another format, add a matching `describe` block directly after the default format's block, e.g. `describe "GET /posts/:id.json"` after `describe "GET /posts/:id"`.
- You MUST NOT add a `describe` block for a Turbo Stream response. Add a `context "with a Turbo Stream"` inside the route's `describe` block, and send `headers: { "Accept" => Mime[:turbo_stream].to_s }` in that context.
- In request specs, send params nested under the singular name, e.g. `post posts_path, params: { post: { title: "Hello" } }`.
- In request specs, give every action's `describe` block at least one scenario for an unauthenticated user, e.g. `context "when not signed in"` that expects a redirect to `new_user_session_path`, or `context "without an access token"` that expects `have_http_status(:unauthorized)` for an API.
- In request specs for another service failing, stub the request to fail with the service's helper from `spec/support` and check the flash, e.g. `stub_newsletter_create_failure` then `expect(flash).to have_flash_alert("Newsletter could not be sent. Please try again later.")`. Stub a timeout the same way, e.g. `stub_newsletter_create_timeout`.
- Name the request spec for a top-level controller that handles actions on a single nested record after its own resource, e.g. `RSpec.describe "Comments"` in `spec/requests/comments_spec.rb` for `CommentsController`.
- Write a request spec for every controller, at the matching path in `spec/requests`, e.g. `spec/requests/posts_spec.rb` for `PostsController` and `spec/requests/posts/comments_spec.rb` for `Posts::CommentsController`. Write one `describe` block for each action, and one for each format the action responds to, e.g. `describe "GET /posts"` then `describe "GET /posts.json"`.
- In each request spec `describe` block, cover every path through the action, happy and sad, e.g. each branch of an `if`, each redirect, and each error the controller rescues. Persona contexts already cover sign-in and authorisation. Inside each context, cover the paths that persona can take.
- Write at least one request spec example for each path, but not one for each reason the path is taken. Leave the detailed cases to model, form and policy specs, e.g. one `it "shows the form again with a blank title"` example for the validation errors in `POST /posts`, and each validation on `Post` in the model spec.
- In request specs, treat each branch in the views an action renders as a path, and write at least one example for it that checks the body, e.g. `it "lists the posts"` and `it "shows a message when there are no posts"` for an `if @posts.any?` in `app/views/posts/index.html.erb`.
- In request specs, you MUST NOT stub the models, forms, actions, services or other classes the action calls, e.g. `allow_any_instance_of(Post).to receive(:publish)` or `allow(Posts::ArchivePost).to receive(:call)`. Check what the action does instead: the records it changes, the response, the flash and the jobs it enqueues. To test how the controller handles an action's `Error`, set up records that make the action fail for real.
- In request specs, you MUST NOT test an action's argument checks, e.g. that `Posts::PublishPost` raises `ActiveModel::ValidationError` for a post with unsaved changes from `unmodified:`.
- In request specs, check that the action enqueues each job with its arguments, e.g. `expect { post post_publication_path(draft) }.to have_enqueued_job(NotifySubscribersJob).with(draft)`. You MUST NOT run the job in a request spec.
- In request specs, stub only the HTTP requests the action makes to other services, and assert that it made them, with the service's stub helpers from `spec/support`, e.g. `newsletter_request = stub_newsletter_create` then `expect(newsletter_request).to have_been_requested`. When a service's SDK has its own stubs, use them instead, e.g. `stub_responses` in the AWS SDK.
- Write at least one feature spec in `spec/features` for every controller that serves pages. Between them, cover the happy path of every HTML route in the controller, e.g. `GET /posts`, `GET /posts/new` and `POST /posts` in `scenario "User writes a post"`. A scenario MAY cover routes from more than one controller. This rule does not cover routes that only serve another format, e.g. `GET /posts.json`, or API controllers, but you MAY write feature specs for them too.
